title: Ultrasonic Testing for Refineries | UT Inspection (US)
description: On-site ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for US refineries: crude, FCC, hydroprocessing and amine units. Send your CML list for a UT quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Refineries: Thickness Surveys and UT Weld Inspection
html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II ultrasonic technicians to refineries across the United States to measure wall thickness on process piping and pressure vessels, examine repair welds, and hand the readings to the owner's API 510 or API 570 inspector. Typical scopes sit on crude, FCC, hydroprocessing, alkylation, sour water and amine units, and are usually planned around a turnaround. To scope a job, request a UT inspection quote.

What ultrasonic testing covers inside a refinery

A refinery runs thousands of piping circuits and hundreds of vessels, and each one is losing metal at some rate. Ultrasonic thickness testing is how that rate becomes a number. We send a sound pulse through the wall, time the echo from the back surface, and record the remaining thickness at a marked location. Repeated over several turnarounds, those readings let the owner's inspector calculate a corrosion rate. That calculation, and the inspection interval that follows from it, belongs to the owner's authorized inspector and engineer, not to us.

The same instruments, with an angled probe, also examine welds for planar flaws such as lack of fusion and cracks. That work shows up when a vessel nozzle is replaced, a piping spool is repaired, or a weld is called into question by another method. We do not offer specialist ultrasonic techniques on this page; the scope is conventional contact UT in the hands of qualified technicians.

Unit by unit: where the metal goes and what we measure

API Recommended Practice 571 describes the damage mechanisms that drive inspection planning. Ultrasonic thickness readings are the evidence that confirms or rules out thinning in each unit.

  • Crude and vacuum units. Naphthenic acid and sulfidation attack hot carbon and low-alloy piping, with the worst wall loss at elbows, tees and reducers where velocity rises. Overhead systems add hydrochloric acid condensation at the first condensing point.
  • FCC units. Erosion from catalyst fines in slurry and flue-gas piping, plus thinning in the main fractionator overhead. Readings on straight runs between elbows tell the inspector whether the loss is general or local.
  • Hydroprocessing units. Ammonium bisulfide in reactor effluent air cooler piping thins carbon steel fast when velocity and concentration drift out of range. Thickness grids across the affected circuits are a standard request.
  • Alkylation units. Acid service thins carbon steel unevenly, so corrosion monitoring points on piping and the acid settler matter. Site safety rules for acid service decide how and when technicians may work.
  • Sour water and amine units. Rich amine piping, regenerator overheads and sour water strippers all lose metal in patterns that follow flow and temperature. We also scan with a straight-beam probe for lamination-type damage in plate exposed to wet hydrogen sulfide.
  • Utilities and offsites. Boiler feedwater, steam condensate, cooling water and tank-farm piping, where thinning is often a slow, steady process.

High-temperature hydrogen attack screening is a specialist job we do not perform. Neither do we inspect furnace tube bundles on this page; for boiler-style tubes see ultrasonic boiler tube inspection.

Piping circuits, condition monitoring locations and API 570

Refinery piping is managed circuit by circuit under API 570 and the owner's mechanical integrity program required by OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119. Each circuit has condition monitoring locations, often called CMLs or TMLs, picked by the owner's piping engineer. Our technicians locate each point from the isometric, clean it, and read it the same way every time, because a reading taken a half inch away from last cycle's reading is not comparable. For circuit-wide surveys, see ultrasonic pipe thickness testing and the piping circuit CML inspection page. API 574 describes the inspection practices behind these surveys, and ASME B31.3 sets the minimum thickness the pipe must retain.

Insulated lines need extra planning. Insulation has to be pulled at each location before we can read the pipe, and the owner's crew must restore it afterward. Where corrosion under insulation is suspected, the inspector decides which locations to open; we report what the metal shows once it is exposed.

Technique details that decide whether readings are usable

  • Calibration. We calibrate on a step block of the same acoustic material as the component, over the thickness range being measured, before each shift and again whenever the instrument or probe changes, following ASME Section V Article 5 and the written procedure.
  • Surface preparation. Scale, loose paint and pitting are removed to bare, smooth metal at each point. Rough, pitted surfaces scatter the signal and produce readings that jump from one visit to the next.
  • Probes. Dual-element probes handle corroded, pitted walls better than single-element probes because they separate transmit and receive paths. For weld examination we use angle-beam probes selected for the thickness and weld geometry.
  • Temperature. Hot lines need high-temperature couplant and probes rated for the surface. Readings on hot metal read slightly thick unless corrected, so the temperature at each point is noted and the correction in the procedure applied.
  • Coverage. For a suspected area of local loss we scan a grid, not a single point, so the minimum thickness is not missed between readings.
  • Weld examination. Shear-wave scanning follows ASME Section V Article 4 and the project procedure; acceptance follows the construction or repair code, usually B31.3 for piping and Section VIII for vessels.

Choosing between UT, MT and PT on refinery components

Which method fits which refinery job
QuestionUTMTPT
Remaining wall on piping or shellYes, the main toolNoNo
Surface cracks on carbon steel weldsLimitedPreferredWorks if surface is clean
Surface cracks on stainless pipingLimitedNot usablePreferred
Lack of fusion buried in a weldYesNoNo
Laminations in plateYesNoNo

For surface cracking on carbon steel, read about magnetic particle inspection for refineries; for stainless and alloy components, liquid penetrant testing for refineries is the sibling page. The comparison in our MT versus PT guide applies directly.

Repairs, alterations and records

Repairs on pressure-retaining equipment follow the National Board Inspection Code or the owner's adopted repair practice, and the examination after a weld repair is specified before the work starts. We ask for that specification up front so the right method and acceptance criteria are on the traveler. When a repaired nozzle or patch plate goes back into service, the baseline thickness taken afterward becomes the starting point for the next corrosion-rate calculation, which is why those first readings are labeled and kept with care.

Under OSHA process safety management, equipment inspection records must show the date, the person who performed the inspection, the equipment inspected, the method and the results. Our reports are written to supply those fields so the owner can drop them straight into the mechanical integrity file, whether that lives in a database or a binder.

Planning around a turnaround or running unit

Most refinery UT is scheduled around a turnaround, when units are down, isolated and cleared for entry, but external thickness readings on in-service lines also happen between outages. The owner's mechanical integrity group normally sends the scope as a CML list, and our crew is mobilized for the agreed scope and dates. Realities worth planning for in the United States:

  • Site orientation, permits, gas monitoring and, at Gulf Coast ports, TWIC credentials are required before anyone touches a line.
  • Scaffold, rope access or lift access is set by the site; readings at elevation depend on it being ready.
  • Confined-space entry for vessel internals follows the site's permit system, with the owner's attendant and rescue plan.
  • Hydrogen sulfide and benzene exposure limits shape how long a technician can work in a given area.
  • Turnaround schedules shift. Share a priority order so the most critical circuits are read first.

Our turnaround and shutdown page explains how our inspection scopes fit an outage window.

What the report contains

  • Component or circuit identification, tied to the owner's drawing and CML numbers.
  • Procedure number and revision, and the code or specification governing the examination.
  • Instrument, probe, couplant and calibration block, with calibration checks recorded.
  • Technician name and level, with the ASNT Level III who approved the procedure and reviewed the report.
  • Thickness readings by location, with surface temperature, previous readings where supplied, and a thickness grid or sketch for any area scanned.
  • Indications from weld examination, with location, length and amplitude, and accept or reject against the named criteria.

The owner's authorized inspector decides what the numbers mean for remaining life and next inspection date. Atlantis does not calculate remaining life, set intervals or perform fitness-for-service work; the API 570 support page describes the NDE data we supply to that inspector.

What to send us for a quote

  • Drawings, isometrics or the CML list, with line numbers or equipment tags.
  • Material, nominal wall thickness and operating temperature range.
  • Count of locations or circuits, and whether weld examination is included.
  • Governing code or owner specification and the written practice reference.
  • Access details: insulation, scaffold, height, confined spaces.
  • Site address, badging, permit and safety orientation requirements.
  • Your turnaround window, or the dates between which work can be done.

Where we work in the US for refining

Refineries cluster in a few regions, and our technicians travel to your site wherever the unit is. These city pages describe the surrounding industry:

  • Houston: the Ship Channel refineries and their large contractor workforce.
  • Beaumont: the Sabine-Neches refining cluster, along with neighboring Port Arthur.
  • Baton Rouge: refineries along the Mississippi River industrial corridor.
  • Lake Charles: Calcasieu Ship Channel refining and processing.
  • Corpus Christi: crude receiving and refining on the South Texas coast.
  • Los Angeles: California refineries, with state process safety rules layered on federal requirements.
  • Philadelphia: East Coast refining along the Delaware River.
  • Gary and Joliet: Midwest refining around the southern end of Lake Michigan.

Training your own technicians

If your refinery wants its own thickness-testing technicians, we teach UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 theory, with the ultrasonic testing simulator for practice. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A your company certifies its people from its own written practice; we help build that practice through written practice development. The oil and gas NDT training page outlines programs for the sector.

What we do not do on refinery work

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, run in-line inspection tools, or act as the API authorized inspector of record. We do not offer specialist ultrasonic techniques on this page, and we do not calculate remaining life. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

faq.q: What do you need to quote ultrasonic thickness testing on refinery piping?
faq.a: Send the CML list or isometrics, line numbers, material, nominal wall, operating temperature, insulation status, access type and your outage window. With those we can count locations, plan the crew and tell you what is missing.

faq.q: Who decides whether a thickness reading is acceptable?
faq.a: The owner's API 570 or API 510 inspector and engineer decide, using minimum required thickness from the design code and the corrosion rate from repeated readings. We supply the NDE data; we do not set intervals.

faq.q: Can UT be done on a hot or running line?
faq.a: Often yes, with high-temperature couplant and probes rated for the surface, plus a temperature correction. The site sets the safe working limit, and some lines are better read during a shutdown.

faq.q: Is ultrasonic testing the right method for finding cracks?
faq.a: It can find planar flaws inside a weld with an angled probe, but surface cracks are usually easier to find with magnetic particle inspection on carbon steel or liquid penetrant on stainless. A mixed scope is common.

faq.q: Do you read thickness through insulation or coatings?
faq.a: We read bare, prepared metal. Insulation is removed by the owner's crew first, and coating is read through only where the procedure has been demonstrated for that coating.

faq.q: How do repeat readings stay comparable from one turnaround to the next?
faq.a: Each point is marked and tied to the isometric, and the same probe type, calibration approach and surface prep are written into the procedure. Reading the same spot is what makes a corrosion rate meaningful.

faq.q: Are your technicians certified by Atlantis?
faq.a: Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer qualifies and certifies its own personnel from a written practice. Our Level II technicians perform and interpret the work, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports.

faq.q: Do you work at refineries outside Texas and Louisiana?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your site anywhere in the United States, including California, the Mid-Atlantic, the Midwest and the Rocky Mountain region. Remote or small sites need more lead time for logistics.

faq.q: Can you also do magnetic particle or penetrant work on the same visit?
faq.a: Yes. A single crew can combine UT, MT and PT in one mobilization, which saves travel and badging for a turnaround scope that mixes thickness checks with weld surface examination.
